usage: Polite-neutral; reporting you liked someone's post
Asking viewers/followers to like (e.g. a creator's request)
Very casual slang; 박다 ('to ram') = liked enthusiastically
examples: 방금 좋아요 눌렀어요.
I just hit like.
Reporting a simple completed action with 방금 ('just now')
사진 예뻐서 좋아요 눌렀어요.
Your photo was pretty so I liked it.
Give the reason with -아서 before the action
구독하고 좋아요 눌러 주세요!
Please subscribe and hit like!
The set creator-request phrase; 구독 ('subscribe') pairs with 좋아요
nuance: 좋아요 is literally the polite sentence 'it's good / I like it' (좋다 + 요), but on every Korean platform (Instagram, KakaoStory, YouTube, Naver) it is also the FIXED NOUN for the like button — the heart/thumb. So 좋아요 눌렀어요 = '눌렀어요 (I pressed) the 좋아요 (like)'. The natural verb is 누르다 ('to press/click a button'), NOT 치다 or 하다: you press a button, you don't 'do' a like. Among young people you'll also hear the slangy 좋아요 박았어요 (박다 = 'to ram in', i.e. liked hard) and on YouTube creators beg 좋아요 눌러 주세요. The contrast learners must feel: 좋아요 (the button/'like') vs 좋아해요 ('I like it/them' as a feeling, 좋아하다). If you mean 'I liked your post' as an action, it's 좋아요 눌렀어요; 당신을 좋아해요 means 'I have feelings for you' — a totally different, romantic statement. The big English-speaker pitfall is calquing 'I liked it' straight into 좋아했어요, which reads as 'I used to like it (feeling)' and has nothing to do with the button. Default to 존댓말 with anyone you're not close to; drop to 좋아요 눌렀어 only with friends.

usage: Polite-neutral; announcing you'll follow their account
맞팔 = mutual follow; common request between users
Asking someone to follow your account

Tell me your account, I'll follow you.
Chain 계정 알려 주세요 ('tell me your account') then the action
저 팔로우했어요, 맞팔 가능해요?
I followed you — can we follow each other?
Ask for a follow-back with 맞팔 가능해요?
팔로워 천 명 넘었어요!
I passed a thousand followers!
팔로워 ('follower') is the person; note it differs from the act 팔로우

So 'I'll follow you' is 팔로우할게요, but 'I have many followers' is 팔로워가 많아요 — swap them and it sounds wrong. A second must-know is 맞팔 (맞-, 'mutually' + 팔로우): 맞팔해요 / 맞팔 가능해요? means 'follow each other / can you follow back?', which is a whole social ritual on Korean Instagram and X. Another trap: don't say 따라가다 ('to physically follow/tail someone') for SNS — that means literally walking behind a person and sounds creepy; the platform sense is only 팔로우하다.

usage: Asking them to message you privately
examples: 자세한 건 디엠 보낼게요.
I'll DM you the details.
자세한 건 ('as for the details') routes private info to DM
디엠 확인해 주세요, 아까 보냈어요.
Please check your DMs, I sent one earlier.
확인하다 ('to check') is the verb for reading messages
공구 문의는 디엠 주세요.
For group-buy inquiries, DM me.
Sellers route questions to DM; 디엠 주세요 = 'DM me'
nuance: 디엠 is the Korean phonetic spelling of the initials 'DM' (Direct Message) — said dee-em — and it means a private message on Instagram/X, as opposed to a public 댓글 (comment). The natural verbs are 보내다 ('to send') and 주다 ('to give/send to me'): 디엠 보낼게요 ('I'll send a DM'), 디엠 주세요 ('DM me'). To say 'via DM', attach the means particle -으로: 디엠으로 보내 주세요. The key contrast: 디엠 is private/one-to-one, while 댓글 is a public comment under a post and 메시지/문자 usually means an SMS text — don't mix them. On KakaoTalk people instead say 카톡 (보낼게요/주세요). Register: -ㄹ게요 keeps 디엠 보낼게요 polite ('I'll send one, heads-up'); friends say 디엠 보낼게. The English-speaker pitfall is pronouncing/writing it as 'DM' in Latin letters in speech, or calquing 'message' into 메시지 (which can sound like a generic text). Another trap: 디엠 하다 ('to do a DM') exists casually (디엠했어요) but the cleaner, more standard phrasing uses 보내다/주다 with the noun. Also, don't confuse 보내다 (send) with 받다 (receive): 디엠 받았어요 = 'I GOT a DM', the opposite direction.

Saying 디엠 보냈어요 when you mean you received one.

usage: 남기다 ('to leave behind') variant, slightly more formal
Let me know in the comments
Routing replies to the comment section with -로
examples: 궁금한 거 있으면 댓글 달아 주세요.
If you have questions, leave a comment.
-으면 ('if') invites comments conditionally
악플 말고 선플 달아 주세요.
Please post kind comments, not hateful ones.
Contrast 악플 ('hate comment') with 선플 ('kind comment')
댓글 보고 답글 달았어요.
I saw your comment and replied.
답글 ('a reply comment') is the response to a 댓글
nuance: 댓글 means a public comment posted under a post or video — and the idiomatic verb is 달다, literally 'to hang/attach', so a comment is something you ATTACH to a post: 댓글(을) 달다. You can also 남기다 ('leave behind'), so 댓글 남겨 주세요 is a slightly more formal equivalent. The reply to a comment is a 답글 (or 대댓글, 'a comment on a comment'). Two culturally loaded relatives: 악플 (악-, 'malicious' + 리플) = a hate comment, and 선플 (선-, 'good') = a kind one; you'll see 악플 금지 ('no hate comments') everywhere. Contrast with 디엠 (private) and 좋아요 (the like button) — 댓글 is specifically the public written remark. Register: 달아 주세요 is the standard polite request; friends get 댓글 달아 줘. The English-speaker pitfall is using 쓰다 ('to write') — 댓글 써 주세요 is understandable but natives strongly prefer 달다/남기다 for comments; 쓰다 fits writing a whole post (글 쓰다), not attaching a comment. Another trap: 댓글 vs 후기/리뷰 — a 후기 is a review (of a product/place), while 댓글 is just a remark under content. Don't say 코멘트; Koreans use the native-feeling 댓글.

usage: 걸다 ('to hang') = paste a clickable link somewhere
Telling someone to click through; 타고 들어가다 ('enter via')
examples: 그 영상 링크 보내 주세요.
Send me the link to that video.
Name the thing (그 영상) then ask for its 링크
프로필에 링크 걸어 놨어요.
I've put the link in my profile.
걸어 놨어요 ('have hung it up') = posted a standing link
링크 클릭하면 바로 신청돼요.
If you click the link, you can sign up right away.
클릭하다 ('to click') + 신청되다 ('gets applied')
nuance: 링크 is the loanword 'link' (a URL/clickable address). Its verbs differ by what you're doing: to SEND someone a link you 보내다 (링크 보내 주세요); to POST/embed a clickable link somewhere you 걸다, literally 'to hang' (링크 걸어 주세요 / 링크 걸어 놨어요), which is the idiom for pasting a link into a bio, comment, or chat; to CLICK it you 클릭하다 or, very naturally, 링크 타고 들어가다 ('enter by riding the link through'). The contrast learners need: 보내다 vs 걸다 — 보내다 delivers it to a person, 걸다 plants it in a public spot. Don't confuse 링크 with 주소 ('address'): a web 주소 is the URL text itself, while 링크 implies the clickable connection, though casually they overlap (링크/주소 보내 주세요 both work). Register: -주세요 is polite; friends get 링크 보내 줘. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 링크 줘 보내 incorrectly ordered, or using 붙이다 ('to stick/paste') as in 'paste the link' — 붙여넣다 is fine for the clipboard action of pasting text, but to make a live link visible to others Koreans say 걸다. Another trap: 링크 열다 ('open the link') is fine but for 'click through and sign up', 링크 타고 들어가세요 sounds far more native.

Korean puts the verb last: 링크 보내 줘 (casual) / 링크 보내 주세요 (polite). The object comes before the verb.
Using 보내다 when you mean post a clickable link publicly.
보내다 sends it to a person. To embed a live link in a bio/comment, use 걸다: 링크 걸어 주세요.
Confusing 링크 with 좋아요 (because both involve buttons).
링크 is a URL you click through; 좋아요 is the like button. 'Send the link' = 링크 보내 주세요, unrelated to liking.

usage: Polite-neutral; standard report of posting media
More natural native verb 올리다 ('to raise/post')
Is it okay if I post the photo?
Asking permission before posting someone's pic
examples: 방금 여행 사진 올렸어요.
I just posted my travel photos.
올리다 is the everyday word natives reach for first
사진 올릴게요, 태그해도 돼요?
I'll post the photo — can I tag you?
태그하다 ('to tag') pairs with posting group pics
용량이 커서 업로드가 안 돼요.
The file's too big so it won't upload.
업로드가 안 되다 ('uploading doesn't work') for a failure
nuance: There are two words for posting media and you should know both. 업로드(하다) is the English loanword 'upload' — common, neutral, slightly techie, and the word you'll see on buttons and for file transfers (especially when something 'won't upload', 업로드가 안 돼요). But the everyday, native-feeling verb Koreans actually say for putting a photo/post on SNS is 올리다, literally 'to raise/put up': 사진 올렸어요. They're interchangeable in meaning, but 올리다 sounds warmer and more natural in conversation, while 업로드 leans technical. The contrast learners need: 올리다 (post it up, for people to see) vs 다운로드/내려받다 (download, the opposite direction) — don't say 업로드 when you mean saving TO your phone. Also distinguish 올리다 (post) from 보내다 (send privately): you 올리다 a public post but 보내다 a DM. Register: -었어요/-ㄹ게요 polite; friends get 올렸어/올릴게. The English-speaker pitfall is over-relying on 업로드 for everything social — using the loanword for a casual Instagram post sounds stiff; prefer 사진 올렸어요. Another trap: the irregular conjugation 올리다 → 올려요/올렸어요 (not 올리어요). And 게시하다 ('to post/publish') exists but is formal/officialese — fine for a notice board, too stiff for chatting about your selfie.

Saying 업로드 when you mean download.

Saying 사진 올리어요 (wrong conjugation).

usage: Checking if they saw it (stories disappear in 24h)
I'll put it on my story
examples: 아까 스토리 올렸는데 봤어요?
I posted a story earlier — did you see it?
-는데 softly links your post to the question
이 사진 스토리에 올려도 돼요?
Can I put this photo on my story?
Ask permission with 올려도 돼요? before posting someone
스토리 캡처해서 보내 줄게요.
I'll screenshot the story and send it.
캡처하다 ('to capture/screenshot') for saving a story
nuance: 스토리 is 'story' — the disappearing 24-hour post format on Instagram (and 카카오스토리 historically). Enter the 6-digit code.

english: I want to grow my followers
usage: I want to grow my followers
Polite-neutral; talking about building an audience
Intransitive 늘다 ('to increase on its own')

You have to post steadily to gain followers.
꾸준히 ('steadily') + the condition -아야 ('only if')
팔로워 만 명 되는 게 목표예요.
My goal is to hit 10,000 followers.
만 명 ('10,000 people') with 명 as the people counter

Crucially Korean splits transitive vs intransitive: 늘리다 = 'I make them increase' (I grow my followers), while 늘다/늘어나다 = 'they increase (on their own)' — so 'my followers went up' is 팔로워가 늘었어요 (intransitive), but 'I want to grow my followers' is 팔로워를 늘리고 싶어요 (transitive, your action). Another trap: -고 싶다 ('want to') attaches to YOUR own desire only — you can't use 팔로워 늘리고 싶어요 about someone else's wish; for a third person it becomes 늘리고 싶어해요. I reported this account and blocked it right away.

usage: Polite-neutral; sellers routing questions to DM
자세한 ('detailed') scopes which questions go to DM
Steering away from public 댓글 to private 디엠
examples: 가격 문의는 디엠으로 주세요.
For price inquiries, please DM me.
가격 문의 ('price inquiry') is the most common DM ask
공구 참여는 디엠으로 문의해 주세요.
To join the group-buy, please inquire by DM.
공구 ('group buy') context; 참여 ('participation')
재고 문의 주셔서 감사해요, 디엠 확인해 주세요.
Thanks for asking about stock — please check your DM.

usage: Asking people to spread your post
I shared it to my story
Reposting to your story with destination -에
examples: 이 글 좋아서 공유했어요.
I liked this post so I shared it.
-아서 ('because') links the reason to the share
친구한테 링크 공유했어요.
I shared the link with a friend.
공유 takes -한테 ('to a person') for who you sent it to
많이 공유해 주세요, 널리 알려야 해요.
Please share it widely — we need to spread the word.
널리 알리다 ('spread far') is why you ask for shares

'I shared the post' = 글 공유했어요; to ask others to spread it, 공유 좀 해 주세요. The destination/recipient particles matter: -에 for a place you repost TO (스토리에 공유했어요, 'shared to my story'), -한테/에게 for a PERSON you send it to (친구한테 공유했어요, 'shared with a friend'). The contrast learners need: 공유하다 (share/spread to many, the SNS button) vs 보내다 ('to send' one-to-one privately) vs 퍼가다 ('to take/grab and repost', the older blog-era word for copying content to your own page). For modern SNS, 공유하다 is the default; 퍼가다 sounds dated or implies lifting someone's content. Don't confuse 공유 with 좋아요 (like) — sharing actively redistributes, liking just reacts. usage: I went ahead and blocked them
-아 버리다 adds 'just did it, done with it'
차단 풀다 ('release the block') = undo a block
examples: 계속 귀찮게 해서 차단했어요.
They kept bothering me so I blocked them.
귀찮게 하다 ('to pester') + the reason ending -아서
스팸 번호라서 바로 차단했어요.
It was a spam number so I blocked it right away.
차단 works for phone numbers too, not just SNS
싸우고 나서 차단당했어요.
After we fought, I got blocked.
차단당하다 ('to be blocked'), the passive — it happened to you
nuance: 차단(하다) (Sino-Korean 遮斷, 'to cut off/block') is the verb for blocking someone — on SNS, KakaoTalk, or your phone — so they can't contact you or see you. 'I blocked them' = 차단했어요; to undo it, 차단 풀다 ('release the block', 차단 풀었어요). The active/passive split is crucial: 차단하다 = YOU block someone, 차단당하다/차단되다 = you GET blocked (it happened to you) — 차단당했어요 means 'I was blocked', the opposite victimhood. Korean adds emotional color with 차단해 버렸어요 (-아 버리다 = 'just did it decisively, good riddance'). The contrast learners need: 차단 (block, total cut-off — they vanish from your world) vs 언팔 (unfollow, you just stop seeing them but no wall) vs 신고 (report, flag to the platform). These are escalating: unfollow < block < report. Don't confuse 차단 with 삭제 ('delete', e.g. delete a friend/contact) — blocking walls them off, deleting just removes the entry. Register: -했어요 polite; friends get 차단했어.
